title: The Axial Age: Buddha, Confucius, Socrates

cards.h: Why did great thinkers pop up everywhere at once?
cards.b:
Between about 800 and 200 BCE, in India, China, Greece and Iran, people began to ask: how should we live? What is a good ruler? What happens after death?

The German philosopher Karl Jaspers noticed this in 1949 and called it the Axial Age, a hinge of history.

Siddhartha Gautama, later the Buddha, was born in a Shakya clan family in Lumbini. His dates are debated: traditionally about 563-483 BCE, but many scholars now place his death between 410 and 400 BCE.

According to tradition, he left home to seek an end to suffering. After years of search, he awakened at Bodh Gaya and taught the Middle Way, between luxury and extreme self-denial.

cards.h: The teacher who wanted good order
cards.b:
Confucius (551-479 BCE) lived in a time when China's states were fighting. He taught that peace comes from good behaviour, respect for family and rulers who set an example. His sayings were collected by students in the Analects.

He was not a success in his lifetime. He never got the high office he hoped for.

cards.h: The man who only asked questions
cards.b: Socrates (470-399 BCE) wrote nothing. We know him from Plato and Xenophon. He walked around Athens asking people to explain what they claimed to know, and embarrassed many. In 399 BCE an Athenian jury of 500 found him guilty of impiety and corrupting the young. He drank hemlock.

In India, the Upanishads and the Jain teacher Mahavira (traditionally 6th century BCE) appeared. In China, Laozi (a possibly legendary figure) is linked with the Daodejing. In Iran, Zoroaster taught about good and evil. In Israel, prophets such as Isaiah wrote.

None of them seems to have known the others.

Ideas proposed: iron tools, growing trade, bigger states and cities, and cruel wars made people search for meaning. Money and writing helped ideas to spread.

But nothing proves any single cause.

Critics say the Axial Age is neat but artificial. The 'age' stretches 600 years. Egypt and Mesopotamia are left out. And many ideas had earlier roots.

Also, a famous slip: the Buddha is sometimes called 'Indian-born'. Lumbini is in present-day Nepal. An inscription on an Ashokan pillar there, from about 249 BCE, says Ashoka visited the Buddha's birthplace.

Five things to remember

  1. Jaspers coined 'Axial Age' in 1949.
  2. Buddha, Confucius and Socrates were near-contemporaries in different places.
  3. Socrates wrote nothing and was executed in 399 BCE.
  4. The Axial Age idea is debated.
  5. Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace, is in Nepal.

Think about it

  • Would these thinkers have survived today's social media?
  • Why do big questions arise in unsettled times?
